title: Rhea Chakraborty's Passport Was Seized in 2020. The Bombay High Court Just Gave It Back. She Was 28. She Is 33.
excerpt: Five years after the SSR case made her the most vilified woman on the Indian internet, the actress holds her passport and posts two words: 'Satyameva Jayate.'
body:
Rhea Chakraborty held up her passport on Instagram this week and wrote two words: "Satyameva Jayate." Truth alone triumphs. Then she added: "Prepared for Chapter 2."

The Bombay High Court ordered the Narcotics Control Bureau to permanently return the actress's passport — seized in September 2020 during the investigation into the death of her boyfriend, actor Sushant Singh Rajput. The court cited her four-year compliance with all legal obligations and noted that similar relaxations had already been granted to eight other accused in the same case.

It took five years.

## What Happened in September 2020

When Sushant Singh Rajput was found dead in his Mumbai apartment on June 14, 2020, three separate investigations were launched — by the CBI, the Enforcement Directorate, and the NCB. Rhea Chakraborty, his girlfriend, became the focal point of a media frenzy that consumed Indian television for months.

The NCB arrested Chakraborty on September 8, 2020, on charges related to procurement and financing of drugs. She spent 28 days in Byculla Women's Jail before being granted bail. Her passport was seized as a bail condition. She was 28 years old.

## The Diaspora's Role in the Storm

What made the Sushant Singh Rajput case unusual was the scale of diaspora engagement. NRI communities — particularly in the United States — organized candlelight vigils, signed petitions, trended hashtags for weeks, and pressured Indian media outlets through coordinated social media campaigns.

The case became a proxy war for multiple grievances: nepotism in Bollywood, the treatment of outsiders, mental health stigma, and media accountability. Rhea Chakraborty was, for a significant portion of the Indian internet and its diaspora extension, the villain of this story.

Five years later, no charges have been proven. The CBI investigation has not resulted in a chargesheet. The NCB case remains in trial. And the woman at the center of it all has spent half a decade unable to leave the country.

## What the Court Said

The Bombay High Court's order was notable for its restraint. Justice [name redacted] observed that Chakraborty had complied with every bail condition for over four years, had attended all hearings, and had not attempted to obstruct the investigation. The court noted that eight other accused in the same case had already received similar relaxations.

The order does not require Chakraborty to seek prior court approval to travel abroad. She must attend trial dates and notify authorities of her travel plans. That's it.

## Chapter 2

Chakraborty's career has been in suspended animation since 2020. Her last film was *Chehre* (2021), an Amitabh Bachchan starrer in which she was conspicuously absent from promotional materials. She has appeared on a few reality shows and launched a podcast, but the kind of roles that were available to her before 2020 — mid-budget Bollywood comedies and dramas — have not materialized.

The passport return changes the practical calculus. International productions, brand endorsements with global campaigns, and the simple act of leaving India for work or leisure are now possible again for the first time since she was 28. She is now 33.

Whether Bollywood will welcome her back is a separate question. The industry that watched her become a national controversy mostly looked away. A few actors — Alia Bhatt, Shibani Dandekar, and Zoya Akhtar — expressed support at different points. Most said nothing.

## The Larger Pattern

Chakraborty's case is part of a broader pattern in which India's criminal justice system uses passport seizure and bail conditions as a form of prolonged punishment before trial. For NRIs watching from abroad — many of whom maintain Indian passports or have family members who do — these cases highlight the gap between accusation and adjudication.

The SSR case consumed the Indian internet for the better part of two years. Five years later, the person most publicly accused has her passport back, no conviction, and an Instagram post that says "Chapter 2."

Whether the audience that once demanded her arrest will now watch her comeback remains the final, unanswered question.
